approaches.name: Direct ulnar approach to the distal ulna
approaches.corridor: Longitudinal interval between extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris

sources.title: Ulnar Approach To The Distal Ulna
The dorsal approach to the distal radioulnar joint

procedure_applications.condition: A distal-ulna or ulnar-styloid fracture requires direct reduction and fixation
Associated distal-ulna instability requires separate fixation after radius reconstruction

positioning.text: Position supine with arm on a radiolucent hand table and forearm neutral or pronated for direct ulnar access and imaging.

setup.text: Assess DRUJ stability, TFCC attachment, and planned implant position; mark the dorsal sensory ulnar-nerve course before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark palpable ulna, ulnar styloid, ECU and FCU tendons, and DRUJ.

incision.text: Make a straight longitudinal incision over the distal ulna between ECU and FCU, centered on the fracture.

superficial_interval.text: Spread subcutaneous tissue carefully, identify and protect the dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve, then enter the ECU-FCU interval.

deep_interval.text: Expose the fracture with limited periosteal stripping and release only the necessary ulnar extensor-retinacular attachment.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous sensory-nerve plane, ECU-FCU interval, extensor retinaculum as needed, periosteum, then distal ulna.

structures_encountered.text: Dorsal sensory ulnar nerve, ECU, FCU, extensor retinaculum, ulnar styloid, TFCC attachment, and distal ulna are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Dorsal sensory ulnar nerve, ECU sheath, ulnar artery and nerve volarly, TFCC, DRUJ cartilage, and distal radioulnar ligaments are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The dorsal sensory branch crosses variably in the subcutaneous plane; identify it rather than relying on a presumed fixed course.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid traction on the sensory branch and circumferential stripping or forceful retraction that destabilizes ECU or TFCC attachments.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to ulnar styloid and distal-ulna fractures and limited access to the DRUJ.

limitations.text: Does not expose the distal-radius articular surface and provides limited deep DRUJ access compared with a dedicated dorsal DRUJ approach.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along the ulna or add a dedicated DRUJ exposure while preserving the dorsal sensory branch and ECU stability.

indications.text: Use for displaced distal-ulna, ulnar-neck, and styloid-base fractures requiring fixation or direct assessment of ulnar-sided stability.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid unnecessary fixation of stable small styloid fragments and choose a DRUJ-specific approach when joint pathology is the primary target.

implant_implications.text: Contour low-profile fixation to avoid ECU irritation and verify screw length and DRUJ/radiocarpal containment.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use PA, lateral, oblique, and DRUJ-focused views to confirm reduction, ulnar variance, implant containment, and radius-ulna congruity.

closure.text: Repair released extensor retinaculum, confirm ECU glide and DRUJ stability, and close without entrapping the dorsal sensory branch.

complications.text: Complications include sensory neuritis or neuroma, ECU irritation or instability, DRUJ stiffness or instability, nonunion, infection, and symptomatic hardware.

bailouts.text: Enlarge under direct nerve control or add a DRUJ-specific window if reduction or stability cannot be assessed safely.

questions.question: Which nerve must be sought?
questions.answer: The dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve.

questions.question: What tissue may require release and repair?
questions.answer: The ulnar attachment of the extensor retinaculum.

approaches.name: Ulnar-palmar approach to the distal radius
approaches.region: ulnar volar wrist and distal forearm
approaches.corridor: Between ulnar neurovascular bundle and flexor tendons, with flexors and median nerve retracted radially

sources.title: Ulnar Palmar Approach To The Distal Radius
Anatomic considerations when performing the modified Henry approach for exposure of distal radius fractures
When is a Volar Plate Not Enough? Indications for Alternative Fixation Techniques in Distal Radius Fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A lunate-facet, sigmoid-notch, volar-ulnar, DRUJ, or high-energy pattern requires direct ulnar-volar control
The approach is extended distally for indicated median-nerve decompression

positioning.text: Position supine with the arm on a hand table and forearm supinated for ulnar-volar access.

setup.text: Map ulnar bundle, median nerve, carpal tunnel, lunate facet and sigmoid notch; prepare magnification and vascular control.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark ulna, wrist crease, pisiform, FCU, palmaris longus, flexor-tendon mass, and ulnar pulse.

incision.text: Begin at the wrist crease parallel to the ulna and extend proximally; extend across the crease into palm when carpal-tunnel or radiocarpal access is required.

superficial_interval.text: Identify the ulnar artery and nerve and develop the plane between them and the flexor tendons.

deep_interval.text: Retract flexor tendons and median nerve radially, expose pronator quadratus, and elevate only the ulnar portion required to reach distal radius.

layers.text: Skin, palmar fascia, ulnar bundle-flexor interval, flexor layer with median nerve, pronator quadratus, then volar-ulnar radius.

structures_encountered.text: Ulnar artery and nerve, flexor tendons, median nerve, pronator quadratus, lunate facet, sigmoid notch, capsule, DRUJ, and distal ulna are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Ulnar artery and nerve, median nerve and palmar cutaneous branch, flexor tendons, palmar radiocarpal ligaments, TFCC, and DRUJ cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Keep the ulnar bundle continuously identified and do not confuse an extensile distal continuation with a complete carpal-tunnel release unless decompression is intended.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid sustained radial traction on median nerve and flexors or ulnar pressure on the neurovascular bundle.

exposure.text: Exposes lunate facet, sigmoid notch, palmar capsule, DRUJ, distal ulna, and carpal tunnel when extended.

limitations.text: Provides poor access to the radial styloid and radial column compared with modified Henry or radial-column approaches.

extensions.text: Extend distally for carpal-tunnel and radiocarpal exposure or combine with radial-volar/dorsal approaches for other columns.

indications.text: Use for isolated lunate-facet and volar-ulnar fragments, sigmoid-notch/DRUJ injuries, and selected high-energy fractures requiring extensile ulnar access.

relative_contraindications.text: Use modified Henry for routine radial-column patterns and avoid compromised ulnar-palmar skin or an unmanageable ulnar neurovascular corridor.

implant_implications.text: Supports fragment-specific volar-ulnar fixation; keep hardware clear of flexors, DRUJ, and radiocarpal joint.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use PA, lateral, oblique, tilted lateral, and DRUJ views to verify lunate-facet capture, sigmoid-notch congruity, and screw containment.

closure.text: Repair pronator quadratus when possible, verify flexor glide and ulnar/median nerve function, and close without constricting the bundle.

complications.text: Complications include ulnar or median neuropathy, arterial injury, flexor-tendon irritation, carpal-tunnel symptoms, DRUJ stiffness, joint penetration, and wound problems.

bailouts.text: Add a separate radial or dorsal exposure when other columns remain uncontrolled rather than over-retracting neurovascular structures.

questions.question: What is the key interval?
questions.answer: Between the ulnar artery/nerve and the flexor tendons.

questions.question: Which fragments are best exposed?
questions.answer: The lunate facet and sigmoid-notch/volar-ulnar region.

approaches.corridor: Longitudinal ECU-FCU interval with explicit dorsal sensory ulnar-nerve protection

sources.title: Ulnar Approach To The Distal Ulna
Physeal Fractures of the Distal Ulna: Incidence and Risk Factors for Premature Growth Arrest
Traumatic ulnar physeal arrest after distal forearm fractures in children

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced distal-ulna or physeal fracture requires open reduction or stable fixation

positioning.text: Position supine with arm on a radiolucent hand table and forearm positioned for direct ulnar access.

setup.text: Localize the distal-ulnar physis and DRUJ, assess remaining growth and associated radius injury, and map the dorsal sensory nerve.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark ulna, ulnar styloid, physis under imaging, ECU, FCU, and DRUJ.

incision.text: Make a longitudinal incision over the distal ulna between ECU and FCU, centered on the fracture and kept no longer than needed.

superficial_interval.text: Seek and protect the dorsal sensory ulnar-nerve branch before developing the ECU-FCU interval.

deep_interval.text: Release only necessary ulnar extensor retinaculum and expose the fracture with minimal periosteal and physeal stripping.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous sensory-nerve plane, ECU-FCU interval, retinaculum, periosteum, then distal ulna and physis.

structures_encountered.text: Dorsal sensory ulnar nerve, ECU, FCU, extensor retinaculum, ulnar styloid, distal-ulnar physis, and DRUJ are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Dorsal sensory nerve, ulnar physis and blood supply, ECU sheath, TFCC, DRUJ cartilage, and ulnar neurovascular bundle are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Avoid repeated physeal manipulation, transphyseal thermal injury, and circumferential epiphyseal stripping; distal-ulnar growth arrest can produce major variance and deformity.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid traction on the dorsal sensory branch and forceful ECU or TFCC retraction.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to pediatric distal-ulna, styloid, and physeal fractures while permitting DRUJ assessment.

limitations.text: Does not expose the radius and cannot substitute for longitudinal surveillance after a physeal injury.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along ulna or add a separate radius/DRUJ exposure while preserving nerve and physeal tissues.

indications.text: Use selectively for irreducible or unstable displaced distal-ulnar physeal, neck, or styloid injuries requiring open control.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid open exposure when acceptable stable closed reduction is achievable and avoid unnecessary fixation of stable small fragments.

implant_implications.text: Choose low-profile, physeal-respecting fixation, avoid joint penetration, and plan removal when growth or implant position warrants it.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm physeal alignment, ulnar variance, DRUJ congruity, and implant containment on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Repair retinaculum, confirm ECU glide and DRUJ stability, and close without injuring or trapping the dorsal sensory branch.

complications.text: Complications include growth arrest, ulnar variance and deformity, DRUJ instability, sensory neuroma, tendon irritation, infection, and nonunion.

bailouts.text: Use a separate approach for associated radius pathology and institute long-term growth surveillance even after satisfactory fixation.

questions.question: Which nerve branch must be protected?
questions.answer: The dorsal sensory branch of the ulnar nerve.

questions.question: What long-term complication requires surveillance?
questions.answer: Distal-ulnar growth arrest with altered ulnar variance.
